extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, social theory, cultural studies, social psychology, and media/communication studies
extracted.subtask_description: Critical/theoretical analysis of humour that foregrounds ridicule and its social functions; situates classic theories (superiority, incongruity, relief) in historical and ideological context and interrogates common-sense positive accounts. Aimed at developing a social critique rather than an empirical catalogue of jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique common-sense positivity about humour
rubrics_metrics.description: A critical approach takes as its object common-sense assumptions about humour's desirability; do not assume laughter is inherently good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book contrasts 'bossy' critics (who aim to improve laughter) and the 'crazy' critic who questions laughter's assumed goodness; the critic's task is to question what common sense overlooks and conceals, including darker sides of collective laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a historical dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs about humour are historically situated; analysis should trace origins and transformations of ideas about humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter structure models this: review historical theories (Hobbes, incongruity tradition, Victorian relief, Bergson, Freud) to show how present common-sense derives from past intellectual currents and why history helps distance us from our own assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose ideological biases (ideological positivism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and critique ideological patterns (termed 'ideological positivism') that stress humour's positives while repressing negatives such as ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine popular self-help psychology, psychotherapy and academic psychology for a consistent pattern of 'accentuate the positive'; use Marcuse's critique of neo-Freudians as example of how theory can domesticate critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance empirical evidence with theoretical critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of empirical findings about laughter but resist uncritical acceptance; empirical data alone are insufficient for critical social theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provine's empiricist road is acknowledged useful, but the book argues for combining empirical awareness with philosophical/historical critique so that data illuminate rather than determine theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situate theories within wider political, moral and aesthetic contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories of humour should be read as part of broader visions of politics, morality and aesthetics rather than as isolated technical hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superiority theory (Hobbes) arises from fearful political vision; incongruity theories reflect gentlemanly tastes; Bergson and Freud must be read in relation to their wider œuvre and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish disciplinary versus rebellious functions of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a humorous act serves rebellious (subversive) purposes or disciplinary (norm-enforcing, ridiculing) functions — and acknowledge that both can coexist or be hard to separate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 9 develops this distinction and stresses the dialectic between humour's capacity to rebel and its power to discipline; practitioners should examine evidence for both functions in any instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze ridicule as a central disciplinary mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how ridicule operates to uphold norms, enforce conformity, and socialize individuals — potentially making it a core mechanism of social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book argues ridicule ensures routine compliance with customs and habits; assess learning-to-ridicule, means of socialisation, and links between ridicule and embarrassment/losing face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to the rhetorical/social nature of laughter (laughter vs 'unlaughter')
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat laughter as a rhetorical, interactional phenomenon whose meaning depends on the possibility of its opposite ('unlaughter'); analyse how laughter conveys approval by contrast with disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 8 emphasizes laughter's rhetoric — consider how laughter functions in interaction (mitigation, approval, display) rather than only as internal affect or reflex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for absences and omissions in theoretical accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique should search for significant absences as well as presences in past and current theories (what ideas are omitted or repressed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical critique to reveal omissions (e.g., many modern psychological accounts overlook the role of ridicule); the book models looking for 'textual repression' of negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an interdisciplinary perspective — avoid narrow specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding humour requires knowledge beyond specialist empirical studies; draw on social/political history, psychology, sociology, cultural studies and theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.L.R. James' epigram ('What do they know of cricket who only cricket know?') is invoked: humour experts need broader knowledge of seriousness and social life to understand comedic reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize primary phenomena over accumulating data
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorizing should aim to distinguish primary from secondary phenomena and order ideas, rather than merely amassing details and data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against purely empirical accumulation that overwhelms broader pattern; theoretical simplicity can direct attention to overlooked phenomena (e.g., ridicule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claims of universality and necessity of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: When a theory claims humour is universal or necessary, scrutinize the evidence and theoretical grounds for such claims and consider alternative explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book proposes humour is central and necessary for social life (not merely adornment); readers should test such explanatory claims against historical, cross-cultural and theoretical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question therapeutic/self-help positive framings
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess therapeutic and self-help claims that present humour and positive thinking as inherently beneficial, including their ideological effects of promoting individual adaptation over social change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 2 diagnoses a pattern across popular psychology and therapy: the elimination of negatives and encouragement to 'accentuate the positive' — critique how this frames social problems as individual coping issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read classic theories (superiority, incongruity, relief) in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine superiority, incongruity and relief theories not as isolated hypotheses but as historically and ideologically embedded accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapters 3–5 model this approach: each theory is examined in its social/intellectual context (e.g., Hobbes' superiority theory within seventeenth-century politics; Victorian relief in Darwinian context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits of neat categorizations and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not expect or force exhaustive taxonomies separating wit/irony/satire/benign vs malevolent humour; accept conceptual messiness in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author warns against providing crisp definitions to categorize every incident; theoretical work should acknowledge overlaps and ambiguities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat laughter as more than physiology — integrate social/psychological dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond physiological accounts of laughter, investigate cognitive, interactional and social dimensions (motives, rhetoric, reception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While physiological/empirical studies (e.g., Provine) are valuable, the book stresses cognitive processes, interactional uses, and social reception as essential analytic dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to cruelty, malice and the 'dark' side of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly examine cruelty, malice, and the damaging effects of humour (e.g., mockery, racist or aggressive humour) rather than glossing them over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson and Freud are cited for pointing to humour's cruelty and deceptive aspects; researchers should document when humour enforces hierarchy, degrades dignity, or perpetuates prejudice.
